objectives: Describe how enzymes work using the lock and key model
Investigate the effect of temperature and pH on amylase activity
Analyse results to identify optimum conditions for amylase

questions.hint: Think: what type of molecule, and what does it do in a reaction?
questions.a: A biological catalyst made of protein that speeds up chemical reactions without being used up.

questions.q: Name the model that describes how enzymes work.
questions.hint: The enzyme and substrate have complementary shapes.

questions.q: What do we call the molecule that fits into an enzyme's active site?
questions.hint: Think: the enzyme has a specific region where it binds.

questions.q: Give two factors that affect enzyme activity.
questions.hint: Think about what changes the speed of a chemical reaction.
questions.a: Temperature and pH (also: enzyme concentration, substrate concentration).

engage.hook: Your saliva is dissolving your food right now.
engage.content: Amylase is an enzyme found in your saliva. It breaks starch into sugar — starting digestion before you swallow. Today we investigate how temperature and pH change how well it works.
engage.imageDescription: Iodine turning blue-black in presence of starch — before and after amylase
engage.discussionPrompt: What do you predict happens to the enzyme when conditions are too extreme?

definitions.definition: A biological catalyst made of protein
definitions.etymology: Greek: en- (in) + zyme (leaven) — first found in yeast

definitions.definition: The molecule that fits the active site
The specific region where the substrate binds
The conditions where enzyme activity is highest
When the enzyme's 3D shape is permanently changed
An enzyme that breaks starch into maltose

items: Every enzyme has a specific active site shape
Only the matching substrate can bind
Rising temperature → more kinetic energy → more collisions → faster
Above optimum: bonds break → enzyme denatures → active site distorted
Changes charges on active site → affects substrate binding
Too acid or alkaline → denatures the enzyme

learn.heading: Rate of Reaction
learn.example: Colour change at 37°C takes 40 s.  Rate = 1 ÷ 40 = 0.025 s⁻¹

build.q: Why is each tube of starch and amylase kept in a water bath?

options.B: To stop the iodine changing colour

build.explanation: Temperature is the control variable; the water bath holds it steady.

build.q: Which iodine result shows the starch has all been broken down?
build.explanation: Iodine stays orange-brown when no starch is left.

build.q: Which statement correctly describes enzyme denaturation?

options.A: The enzyme runs out of substrate and stops working
options.B: The active site permanently changes shape so substrate cannot bind
options.C: The enzyme slows down temporarily at low temperatures
options.D: The substrate breaks down before it can reach the enzyme

build.explanation: Denaturation permanently alters the active site shape — the enzyme cannot function even if conditions return to normal.
build.commonError: C describes inhibition at low temperature, not denaturation — the key word is permanent.

build.q: What is the substrate for amylase?
build.explanation: Amylase is a carbohydrase — its substrate is starch, which it breaks into maltose.

build.q: Which reagent tests for starch, and what colour change indicates it is absent?
build.explanation: Iodine goes blue-black with starch present. Orange-brown means no starch — amylase has broken it all down.

build.q: A student tests amylase at 80°C. What result should she expect and why?

options.A: Fast breakdown — high temperature means more energy
options.B: No breakdown — enzyme is denatured above optimum
options.C: Slow breakdown — enzyme activity reduces with heat
options.D: Normal breakdown — enzymes are not affected by extreme temperatures

build.explanation: 80°C is well above amylase's optimum of 37°C. The enzyme denatures — active site changes permanently, starch cannot break down.

build.setup: A student heats amylase to 80°C then adds starch. She adds iodine after 10 minutes.
build.prediction: Will the iodine turn blue-black or stay orange-brown?
build.reveal: Blue-black — starch is still present. The enzyme was denatured at 80°C and could not break down the starch.
build.explanation: At 80°C heat breaks the bonds maintaining the enzyme's 3D shape. The active site is permanently distorted. Starch can no longer bind.
build.commonError: Students often predict orange-brown — they confuse high temperature = fast reaction, forgetting that above optimum causes denaturation.

build.title: Amylase and Starch — Effect of Temperature
build.intro: Investigate the effect of temperature on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch.
steps: Add 5 drops of iodine solution to each well of a spotting tile
Set up water baths at 20°C, 37°C and 60°C
Mix 1 cm³ amylase with 1 cm³ starch solution in a test tube
Place tube in water bath and start the timer immediately
Every 30 s, transfer one drop to a spotting tile well using a pipette
Record the time when iodine no longer turns blue-black
Repeat for each temperature — clean equipment between trials
build.warning: Iodine stains skin and clothing. Wear goggles throughout.

questions.q: Why do we test drops on the spotting tile rather than adding iodine directly to the test tube?
questions.a: To avoid contaminating the reaction mixture — iodine would interfere with the enzyme and starch.

questions.q: What does it mean when the iodine stays orange-brown?
questions.a: No starch is present — amylase has broken it all down into maltose.

questions.q: Why might the 60°C test take much longer or not complete at all?
questions.a: At 60°C the enzyme may partially or fully denature — fewer active sites available, reaction slows or stops.

worked.prompt: At 37°C the colour change took 40 seconds. Calculate the rate of reaction.

yourTurn.prompt: At 20°C the colour change took 120 seconds. Calculate the rate.

build.graphLabel: Rate of amylase activity vs Temperature

questions.q: At what temperature is amylase most active? Name this temperature.
Describe and explain what happens to the rate above 37°C.
questions.a: Rate decreases rapidly. High temperature breaks bonds in the enzyme's structure — the active site denatures and substrate can no longer bind.

questions.q: Predict the rate at 100°C. Explain using the lock and key model.
questions.a: Rate ≈ 0. Enzyme fully denatured — active site shape has permanently changed, substrate cannot bind.

developing.q: Name the enzyme that digests starch.
What colour does iodine turn when starch is present?
What happens to a denatured enzyme's active site?
developing.a: The active site permanently changes shape — the substrate no longer fits.

reaching.q: Explain why amylase works fastest at 37°C but not at 70°C.
reaching.a: At 37°C there is enough kinetic energy for frequent enzyme-substrate collisions. Above 37°C, excessive heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape — the active site denatures permanently — so substrate cannot bind and the reaction rate falls to zero.

reaching.q: A student calculates rate at pH 4 = 0.005 s⁻¹ and at pH 7 = 0.025 s⁻¹. How many times faster is amylase at pH 7?
A student repeats the experiment at 37°C three times and gets times of 38 s, 40 s and 45 s. Calculate the mean rate of reaction.

mastering.q: Evaluate the experimental design. Suggest two improvements with reasoning.
mastering.a: 1. Repeat 3 times and calculate mean — reduces effect of random errors and anomalous results. 2. Control all other variables (volume of enzyme and starch, same batch of iodine) — ensures only temperature/pH is the independent variable, making it a fair test.

mastering.q: The student finds rate at 60°C is lower than at 20°C. This is unexpected. Suggest and justify an explanation.
mastering.a: At 60°C the enzyme has partially or fully denatured — fewer functional active sites. Despite more kinetic energy, fewer successful enzyme-substrate complexes form per second. At 20°C the enzyme is intact, so even with less kinetic energy more functional active sites are available.

mastering.q: Predict the effect on rate if substrate concentration is doubled. Justify using collision theory.
mastering.a: Rate increases. More substrate molecules means more frequent enzyme-substrate collisions per unit time, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form per second — provided the enzyme is not saturated.
